did_you_know.text: Did you know? The prophecy in this chapter is addressed to the mountains of Israel, which are described as able to hear the word of the LORD.
Did you know? The LORD describes the surrounding nations and Edom as rejoicing over the land’s destruction and wanting to take possession of it.
Did you know? The restoration of the land is described through a direct address to the mountains: the LORD will turn to them, and they will be cultivated and sown again.
Did you know? One of the promises of restoration is that the land will be populated with people and animals, returning to its former condition and becoming even better than before.
Did you know? The chapter presents Israel’s exile as the result of defiling the land through bloodshed and idolatry, and then describes how the LORD’s name was profaned among the nations.
Did you know? The LORD emphasizes that he is acting not because of Israel’s merits, but for the sake of his holy name, which was profaned among the nations.

Did you know? The process of renewal includes not only gathering the people from the nations and bringing them back to the land, but also cleansing them with pure water from all their impurities and idols.
Did you know? The change of heart in this chapter is described as removing a heart of stone and replacing it with a heart of flesh—a metaphor for a more sensitive inner transformation.
Did you know? After placing his Spirit within Israel, the LORD promises that they will follow his statutes, keep his judgments, and carry them out.
Did you know? The land that had been desolate is described after its restoration as looking like the Garden of Eden, while the ruined cities are described as fortified and inhabited.
